query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The high-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA under oxidizing or reducing exposures is governed by the rate‐limiting outward diffusion of Al through the fcc matrix to form a protective α‐Al2O3 scale and the concurrent segregation of Ti to grain boundaries that nucleates discrete TiO2 islands, which disrupt scale continuity. The baseline alloy’s Al content lies near the critical Al/Cr threshold for continuous alumina formation, leading to mixed, partly nonprotective oxide layers, spallation in air, and internal Ti‐driven oxidation in reducing atmospheres.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐built, additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy with a single‐phase fcc microstructure and typical AM grain boundary density.
generation.intervention: Increase Al content from 0.20 to 0.25 (i.e. Al0.25Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3) in an otherwise identical AM process to raise the Al/Cr ratio above the α‐Al2O3 formation threshold.
generation.conditions: Isothermal exposures at 800 °C for 100 h in (a) laboratory air (pO2≈0.21 atm) and (b) a reducing H2/H2O mixture (pO2≈10–18 atm).
generation.structural_mediator: Al flux through the fcc lattice and along grain boundaries; Ti segregation and TiO2 precipitation at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: At 800 °C in air, formation of a continuous α‐Al2O3 scale is limited by Al diffusion in the high‐entropy fcc matrix; Ti that migrates to boundaries forms discrete TiO2 islands that interrupt scale cohesion and promote spallation. In reducing atmospheres, low oxygen partial pressures suppress continuous oxide scale growth, enabling subsurface internal oxidation of Ti at grain boundaries and embrittlement.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al‐enriched (Al0.25…) variant will form a continuous, adherent α‐Al2O3 scale yielding ≈50% lower oxidation mass gain and negligible spallation in air, and will show significantly reduced internal Ti oxidation and better retention of mechanical integrity in the reducing environment, compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Baseline Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy exhibits mixed Al2O3/Cr2O3 scales with local scale spallation (mass gain >1 mg/cm2 after 100 h in air) and pronounced internal Ti oxide clustering in reducing atmospheres.
generation.boundary: Temperatures of 700–900 °C, exposure durations up to 100 h, oxygen partial pressures between 10–19 and 1 atm.
generation.uncertainty: ±20% in predicted mass‐gain reduction; the exact Al/Cr threshold for continuous alumina formation in the AM microstructure may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two AM HEA variants—baseline Al0.2… and Al0.25…—with identical microstructures. Expose both to 800 °C/100 h in air and H2/H2O (pO2≈10–18 atm).
measurements: Cross‐sectional SEM/EDS mapping for oxide continuity and TiO2 dispersion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al‐enriched variant shows mass gain within ±10% of the baseline in either atmosphere, exhibits mixed or discontinuous alumina scales, or displays equivalent internal Ti oxidation, then the hypothesis is falsified.
